thesis: What changed since last tick is that the AI-capex de-rating this book has been trading around for two ticks widened from spending announcements into the supply chain itself: on 7/28 the semiconductor complex cratered on its own — MU -8.9%, ARM -8.1%, AMD -8.1%, MRVL -7.8%, INTC -5.8%, ASML -4.4%, QCOM -4.2% — not because any of them raised capex, but on reports that Chinese memory maker CXMT is preparing an $8.55B IPO, that AI cloud provider CoreWeave is exploring hedges against falling memory prices, and (for ASML specifically) that a Chinese state-backed firm has begun mass-producing chipmaking equipment. This is notably not a rates story: the 10-year eased a third straight session to 4.62% on falling oil, which should help duration-sensitive growth names — so the selloff is genuine AI-trade-specific skepticism, one step further downstream from where the book was already positioned defensively. The same session, capital visibly rotated into biotech/pharma: AMGN, GILD, VRTX, REGN, UNH and LLY all rallied together, consistent with reporting that the sector's trailing-year return (>56%) is running more than double the Nasdaq 100's. This book already owned LLY for reasons unrelated to that rotation (the orforglipron franchise) and is adding a second, smaller biotech leg in VRTX (5%) ahead of its own 8/3 print, sized below LLY/PYPL specifically because the VRTX thesis leans more on the sector tailwind than a name-specific edge — flagged plainly as this tick's one rotation-following trade rather than an anticipation trade. PYPL delivered on both of its legs at once: a Q2 beat-and-raise (EPS $1.38 vs $1.28 est, revenue $8.7B vs $8.48B est, FY guidance raised to $5.38) that popped the stock 4.0% on top of the M&A spread, with Stripe/Advent reportedly pushing to close a deal before month-end — but RSI(14) at 78.9 after that pop is the most extended reading in the book, so it is trimmed 14% to 12% to lock part of the move without abandoning the position (and for the record, this is a short-window overbought signal, not a 52-week-high one: Robinhood's fundamentals show the real 52-week high is $79.50 from 2025-07-28, so the stock is still 26.6% below it — a correction to how the prior report's limited price window described this). BAC gets the same treatment at smaller scale — RSI 70.7, a fresh 52-week high set 7/27, no catalyst until October — cut 5% to 3%, applying the RSI-70 trim rule proactively rather than retroactively, which the prior reflection flagged as a gap between diagnosis and action. The energy pair is cut again, 4/4 to 3/3: the Brent premium that justified holding it as a hedge kept fading (down to roughly $85-89 from $96.78 four sessions ago) even as both names' RSI cooled from the most overbought readings in the universe back toward neutral — the hedge is doing its job and is sized down accordingly, not eliminated, because Middle East risk has cooled, not resolved. The harder admission is REGN and GOOGL: both were sold at the 7/27 open per last tick's decision, and both then ran hard against the exit — REGN +5.1% to 695.29 on a sector-rotation-plus-Telix-collaboration bounce two tick-days before its own 7/30 print, GOOGL +2.7% to 333.73 on recognition of Google Cloud's 82% growth. Neither gets bought back here: REGN's Eylea deterioration (US sales -10% y/y, first sub-$1B quarter since 2018, Citi cut to Neutral/$700) is a real fundamental read that a bounce doesn't resolve, and the print is 2 tick-days out; GOOGL has no scheduled catalyst before Q3 earnings and is still down 5.6% over 20 sessions despite the bounce — buying either now would be exactly the confirmation-chasing this book exists to avoid, even though not chasing has a visible cost already reflected in this tick's numbers. META stays at zero through its own 7/29 print, one tick-day out, where Citi models operating margin compressing to 33.8% from 43.0% on Q2 capex near $33.7B — the same pattern GOOGL/INTC/TSLA/ORCL already confirmed, now facing its real-time test. With FOMC on 7/29 (79.5% priced for a hold, a modest 19.4% priced for a hike, June's dot plot leaning hawkish), MSFT and META reporting 7/29 after close, AAPL and AMZN 7/30 after close, REGN 7/30, and XOM/CVX 7/31 — five dated events in the next three tick-days — the 63% cash buffer stays exactly the size it was last tick, reallocated only within the deployed 37%.

reflection.looking_back: The 7/24 tick queued six changes to the prior 8-name book: cut META, REGN and GOOGL to zero, trim BAC 10%->5%, cut XOM/CVX from 16.8% to an 8% hedge, and raise PYPL 6%->14% and LLY roughly 8%->10%. All orders filled at the next session's open, 7/27 (a weekend intervened). Marking the resulting target book (PYPL 14, LLY 10, BAC 5, XOM 4, CVX 4, 63% cash) forward from observed closes — not yet the confirmed settlement record, since no tick has run between 7/24 and this one — gives an estimated book return of roughly +0.4% from 7/24 close to 7/28 close, against SPY's +0.25% (738.93 -> 740.76) over the same two sessions. That is a small positive alpha, but a much thinner edge than the +1.08-point result logged two ticks ago, and it is almost entirely a single-stock (PYPL) story rather than a broad one.
worked: PYPL, the prior tick's own stated anchor, delivered on both legs simultaneously: Q2 EPS of $1.38 beat the $1.28 estimate, revenue of $8.7B beat $8.48B, and FY guidance was raised to $5.38 EPS — the stock gained 4.0% on 7/28 (56.07 -> 58.32) on top of the shares added at the 7/27 open (56.36), roughly a +3.5% gain on the incremental position within two sessions.

The XOM/CVX re-labeling as a fading hedge rather than an earnings trade was vindicated on the facts, not just the framing: Brent kept falling, from the $96.78 close cited last tick to roughly $85-89 by 7/28, as easing Middle East conflict signals took the geopolitical premium out of the market. XOM's RSI cooled from 84.0 to 62.1 and CVX's from 92.0 to 56.4 — the overbought reading corrected exactly as flagged, without needing a hard stop.

LLY's addition ahead of its own 8/5 print caught a genuine, still-running biotech/pharma rotation: the position gained roughly 1.5% since the 7/27 fill, on a session (7/28) where AMGN, GILD, VRTX, REGN and UNH all rallied together as capital left semis for healthcare.
missed: REGN was cut to zero at the 7/27 open (661.77) on the Eylea deterioration + Citi downgrade thesis, and the stock then ran to 695.29 by 7/28 close — a 5.1% move against the exit, on a session where it was also flagged as a fresh 20-day breakout in the re-screened universe. The fundamental read (US Eylea -10% y/y, first sub-$1B quarter since 2018) may still be right into the 7/30 print, but selling the same tick a downgrade fully de-risks the price is a worse exit than waiting would have been.

GOOGL's residual position was also sold at the 7/27 open (325.04) — the second sell in two ticks — and the stock kept climbing to 333.73 by 7/28 close, a further 2.7% move against the exit. GOOGL is still down 5.6% over 20 sessions and carries no scheduled catalyst before Q3 earnings, so there was no fresh information driving the second sale; the position was closed on inertia from the capex-selloff thesis rather than a live reason to sell again.

The RSI-extension discipline adopted for energy last tick ('treat overbought as a reason to trim') was not applied to BAC or PYPL until this tick, even though BAC (RSI 70.7, a fresh 52-week high set 7/27) and PYPL (RSI 78.9 post-earnings) both crossed the same threshold within days — the lesson was applied to one sleeve and not carried across the whole book.
reflection.adjustment: Separate 'is the fundamental read still right' from 'is this the day to press the trade.' Going forward, once a name has already fully repriced on a confirmed negative catalyst and downside momentum visibly stalls (REGN's Eylea miss, GOOGL's capex selloff), cut size but do not sweep the residual to zero into an already-extended reversal without a fresh reason — the discipline that correctly caught GOOGL's post-earnings drop the first time does not automatically repeat on a second sale of the same name. This tick, that shows up as applying the RSI-70+ trim rule proactively to BAC and PYPL rather than waiting for a bad session to justify it, and as declining to chase GOOGL's bounce (no forward catalyst means it is not this book's trade) even though not chasing has a visible, already-realized cost.
